newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surplus won't spark severe friction -- MOF.
newsitem.headline: Japan surplus won't spark severe friction -- MOF.

text.p: Japan's surplus in trade in goods and services is unlikely to grow to an extent that would invite severe trade friction, a Finance Ministry official told reporters on Tuesday.

Briefing reporters ahead of the Group of Seven (G7) nations' summit meeting from June 20 to 22, the official said: "In the short term, I think our trade in goods and services balance will be affected by temporary factors or the relative demand situation in Japan and overseas markets."

He added, however, "Abstracting these various factors from the medium-term perspective, we do not envisage Japan's trade in goods and services surplus will grow to an extent that would invite severe trade friction."

Asked whether Japan's economy could withstand a stronger yen, the official said: "My impression is there hasn't been a strong outcry from the Japanese business side (after the dollar/yen rate moved from 127 yen to the dollar to its current level)."
He also said there was currently no danger that the recovery would be derailed by the Japanese currency's appreciation.
Asked about recent volatility in the foreign exchange markets, the official said, "I think the G7 finance ministers have the view that excessive volatility is undesirable."
He declined, however, to comment on what precisely constituted excessive volatility.
The official also said that, at the G7 summit in Denver, Japan was interested in discussing measures to strengthen the stability of international markets, including the foreign exchange markets.
He said an agreement struck by G7 finance ministers in Washington, D.C. in April was "valid and relevant" for the Denver summit.

Asked whether Japan might reconsider its efforts at fiscal restructuring, the official said, "The prime minister is very clear on that point. Fiscal structural reform is a priority for the (Ryutaro) Hashimoto cabinet."

Commenting on recently released economic data, the official said: "On the whole I think we are encouraged by the (latest) series of macroeconomic indices." He declined to comment, however, on whether the Bank of Japan was therefore likely to raise interest rates soon.

Turning to recent concerns about the outlook for a single European currency, the official said: "My personal view is that European countries continue to be making progress toward the introduction of a single currency and there is fairly firm political commitment to that."
